slides.title: How deep should fiber go?
slides.sub: Depth of cover, and why it matters

slides.title: Ten inches down, a lawn trencher found the fiber.
slides.body: The street lost internet for the afternoon. It was too shallow to survive ordinary life.

slides.title: Depth does four jobs
slides.body: Keeps cable below casual digging, spreads vehicle loads, avoids frost heave, and leaves room for crossing utilities.

slides.title: Commonly seen US minimums
head: Location
Cover
slides.note: The local owner's or permit's rule always governs.

slides.title: Roads keep getting rebuilt
slides.body: Road owners mill, resurface and widen. A crossing that was fine at 24 inches becomes a hazard after reconstruction.

slides.title: India digs much deeper
slides.body: Highway right-of-way rules often specify around 1.65 m, because widening and drainage works are frequent.

slides.title: Can't reach depth? Say so
slides.body: Rock or another utility in the way? Agree a protection method, like concrete encasement, and document it.

caption:
Every extra inch of depth costs digging time, so it gets argued over on every job.

But depth is what keeps fiber away from sprinkler trenches, fence posts and road rebuilds. Swipe for the common minimums, why India digs to 1.65 m on highways, and what to do when you hit rock.
